mainEntity.name: How many types of comments are there in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Java supports exactly three types of comments: (1) Single-line comment using // — everything after // on that line is ignored. (2) Multi-line comment using /* ... */ — everything between the delimiters is ignored, can span multiple lines. (3) Documentation comment using /** ... */ — used with the javadoc tool to auto-generate HTML API documentation.

mainEntity.name: What is a Javadoc comment and how is it different from a regular comment?

acceptedAnswer.text: A Javadoc comment starts with /** (two asterisks) and ends with */. Unlike regular comments which are only for human readers, Javadoc comments are processed by the javadoc tool to auto-generate professional HTML documentation. They support special tags like @param, @return, @throws, @author, @version, and @since to document classes and methods formally.

mainEntity.name: Can you nest multi-line comments in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Multi-line comments (/* ... */) cannot be nested in Java. If you write /* outer /* inner */ end */, the compiler sees the first */ as the end of the comment and tries to parse 'end */' as code — causing a compile error. Use single-line comments (//) when you need to comment out code that already contains multi-line comments.

mainEntity.name: Do Java comments affect program performance?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Java comments are completely stripped out by the compiler before the bytecode is generated. They do not appear in the compiled .class file and have zero effect on runtime performance. You can write as many comments as you want without worrying about slowing down your program.

mainEntity.name: What are the most important Javadoc tags to know?

acceptedAnswer.text: The most commonly used Javadoc tags are: @param (describes a method parameter), @return (describes the return value), @throws or @exception (describes exceptions thrown), @author (names the author), @version (specifies the version), @since (indicates when the element was added), @see (adds a reference link), and @deprecated (marks an element as outdated).

blocks.text: In the previous chapter, we learned about Java Identifiers — the naming rules for variables, methods, classes, and packages. Now we will cover Java Comments — one of the most important but often overlooked habits of a professional developer.

A comment is a line or block of text in your source code that the Java compiler completely ignores. Comments are written for human readers — developers, teammates, or your future self — to explain what the code does, why a decision was made, or to temporarily disable code during debugging.

items.text: All three Java comment types (single-line, multi-line, Javadoc), complete Javadoc tag reference, how to generate HTML documentation, best practices, and common mistakes to avoid.

blocks.text: Good comments are a mark of a professional developer. Here is why comments matter in real-world Java development:

items.title: Explain Intent
items.text: Code shows WHAT is happening. Comments explain WHY — the reasoning behind a decision that may not be obvious from the code itself.

items.title: Team Collaboration
items.text: In a team, others read your code. Clear comments reduce the time teammates spend understanding your logic and reduce review cycles.

items.title: Debugging Aid
items.text: Temporarily comment out a line or block to isolate a bug without deleting code. Uncomment to restore. Faster than Ctrl+Z.

items.title: Auto-generate Docs
items.text: Javadoc comments (/** */) are processed by the javadoc tool to generate professional HTML API documentation — exactly like the official Java API docs.

items.title: Future Maintenance
items.text: Code you write today will be maintained months or years later — possibly by you. Comments save hours of re-understanding your own logic.

items.title: Learning Tool
items.text: Commenting each line as you learn forces you to understand what the code does. A great habit for beginners to build understanding.

items.html: ⚠️ Important: Java comments are completely removed by the compiler before bytecode is generated. They have zero impact on runtime performance — your .class file contains no trace of them.

blocks.text: A single-line comment starts with two forward slashes //. Everything from // to the end of that line is ignored by the compiler. It is the most commonly used comment type in Java.

blocks.text: Here is a quick side-by-side reference of all three Java comment types so you know exactly when to use each one:
Writing comments well is a skill. Here are the professional best practices followed in industry-grade Java codebases:

items.title: Comment WHY, not WHAT
items.text: Code already shows what is happening. Comments should explain WHY — the business rule, the edge case, the reason for a non-obvious decision.

items.title: Keep Comments Short
items.text: A good comment is concise. If you need a paragraph to explain a few lines of code, consider refactoring — cleaner code needs fewer comments.

items.title: Keep Comments Updated
items.text: Outdated comments are worse than no comments — they actively mislead readers. Always update the comment when you update the code.

items.title: Javadoc All Public APIs
items.text: Every public class, method, and field that others will use should have a Javadoc comment. This is a mandatory standard in professional teams.

items.title: Avoid Obvious Comments
items.text: Don't write: // increment i by 1 above i++; — this adds noise. Write comments for logic that isn't immediately obvious to another developer.

items.title: Use TODO and FIXME
items.text: // TODO: add input validation and // FIXME: crashes when input is null are recognized by most IDEs and flag pending work clearly.

blocks.label: Good vs Bad Comments
lines: // ❌ BAD — states the obvious, adds no value
int age = 21;  // minimum age to open a bank account per RBI guidelines
// 86400 = seconds in a day; reset session after 24 hours
// TODO: replace this linear search with binary search for large datasets
// FIXME: throws NullPointerException when user is not logged in

blocks.text: Even experienced developers make comment mistakes. Here are the most common pitfalls and how to avoid them:

rows: The first */ ends the outer comment — compile error
Use // to comment out code containing /* */
// returns user age (code now returns username)
Misleads every developer who reads it
Update the comment whenever you change the code
Clutters the codebase — unclear if it's needed
Delete it; use Git history to recover if needed
Javadoc on private members without purpose
Private fields rarely need Javadoc — adds noise
Reserve Javadoc for public APIs; use // for private notes
/** Adds two numbers. */ public int add(int a, int b)
Users of your API don't know what a and b mean
The // has no effect inside /* */; entire block is commented

blocks.label: Nested Comment Mistake — Compile Error
lines: * Attempting to comment out a block that contains another block comment:
* int x = calculate(); /* uses old formula */
* Java sees THIS as the end of the outer /* comment
* Everything after this is treated as live code → compile error!
// ✅ Correct way to comment out code that has /* */ inside:
// int x = calculate(); /* uses old formula */

blocks.text: Let us write one complete, professional Java program that demonstrates all three comment types used in the right context — exactly as you would write them in a real-world project.

lines: * Represents a simple bank account with deposit and withdrawal operations.

/** Minimum balance required to keep the account active (in rupees). */
/** The current balance of the account. */
/** The name of the account holder. */
* Creates a new BankAccount with an initial deposit.
* @param holderName    the name of the account holder; must not be null
* @param initialAmount the opening balance; must be >= {@value MIN_BALANCE}
* @throws IllegalArgumentException if initial amount is below minimum balance
// Validate the initial deposit before setting
"Opening balance must be at least ₹" + MIN_BALANCE
* Deposits the given amount into the account.
* @param  amount  the amount to deposit; must be positive
* @throws IllegalArgumentException if amount is zero or negative
* Business rule: deposits must be positive.
* A zero deposit is meaningless and negative would be equivalent

* @throws IllegalArgumentException if amount exceeds available balance

"Insufficient funds. Minimum balance of ₹" + MIN_BALANCE + " required."
* Returns a formatted account summary string.
* @return account summary with holder name and current balance
return String.format("Account Holder: %s | Balance: ₹%.2f", holderName, balance);

blocks.text: Practice This Code — Live Editor
These are commonly asked Java interview questions related to comments — from basic syntax to tricky edge cases and Javadoc usage.

items.q: Q1. What are the three types of comments in Java? Explain each.
items.a: Java supports three comment types: (1) Single-line comment (//) — everything after // to end of line is ignored; best for short inline notes. (2) Multi-line comment (/* ... */) — spans any number of lines; best for block explanations or disabling multiple lines of code. (3) Documentation comment (/** ... */) — processed by the javadoc tool to generate HTML API documentation; supports @param, @return, @throws tags etc.

items.q: Q2. Do comments affect Java performance? Do they appear in .class files?
items.a: No and No. Java comments are completely stripped by the compiler during compilation. The generated .class (bytecode) file contains no trace of any comment. They have absolutely zero impact on runtime performance, startup time, or memory. You can write as many comments as needed without any concern.

items.q: Q3. Can you nest multi-line comments in Java? What happens if you try?
items.a: No — multi-line comments (/* ... */) cannot be nested in Java. If you write /* outer /* inner */ rest */, the Java compiler treats the first */ as the closing delimiter of the entire comment. Everything after that first */ is parsed as code, causing a compile error. To safely comment out code that already contains /* */, use // on each line instead.

items.q: Q4. What is the difference between /* */ and /** */ in Java?
items.a: Both start multi-line comments, but /** */ (Javadoc) starts with double asterisks and is designed for API documentation. The javadoc tool only processes /** */ comments — it ignores /* */ completely. /** */ supports special @ tags like @param, @return, @throws, @author, @version. IDEs also show /** */ content as hover tooltips when you use a method. Use /* */ for internal code comments and /** */ for public API documentation.

items.q: Q5. What is the javadoc tool and how do you use it?
items.a: javadoc is a command-line tool included in the JDK that reads /** */ comments from your Java source files and generates a set of HTML files forming a professional API documentation website. Basic usage: 'javadoc -d docs ClassName.java' generates docs in a 'docs' folder. Add -author and -version flags to include those tags. Most IDEs (IntelliJ, Eclipse) also have built-in javadoc generation via right-click menu.

items.q: Q6. What Javadoc tags do you use to document a method?
items.a: @param name description — one tag per method parameter. @return description — describes the return value (skip for void). @throws ExceptionType description — documents exceptions the method can throw. @since — when the method was added. @deprecated — marks the method as outdated and suggests an alternative. Inline: {@code text} for code in description, {@link ClassName#method} for clickable cross-references.

items.q: Q7. What is the difference between @throws and @exception in Javadoc?
items.a: There is no practical difference — @throws and @exception are synonymous Javadoc tags that both document exceptions. @throws is the preferred modern tag (introduced in Java 1.2) and should be used in new code. @exception is the older tag and is kept for backward compatibility only. Both generate identical output in the HTML documentation.

items.q: Q8. Is it a good practice to comment out code and leave it in production?
items.a: No — it is considered bad practice. Permanently commented-out code clutters the codebase, confuses other developers (is it needed? why was it disabled?), and never gets cleaned up. The correct approach is to delete unused code — version control systems like Git preserve the full history, so you can always retrieve deleted code via git log or git blame if needed later.

blocks.text: Test your understanding of Java Comments. Answer each question yourself before revealing the answer.

items.q: 1. What is the output of this program? int x = 5; // x = 10; System.out.println(x);
items.a: Output: 5. The // x = 10; part is a single-line comment — the compiler ignores everything after // on that line. So x is never changed from 5. The assignment x = 10 is dead code inside a comment.

items.q: 2. Will this code compile? /* outer comment /* inner comment */ still outer? */ int x = 5;
items.a: No — compile error. The first */ (after 'inner comment') is treated as the closing delimiter of the entire outer comment. The text 'still outer?' is then parsed as Java code — which is not valid syntax. Rule: multi-line comments cannot be nested.

items.q: 3. Which comment type would you use to document a public method in a library that other developers will use?
items.a: Javadoc comment (/** ... */). This is the only comment type processed by the javadoc tool to generate HTML documentation. It also appears as IDE hover tooltips when other developers use your method. You should include @param for each parameter, @return for the return value, and @throws for any exceptions.

items.q: 4. What is the output? System.out.print("A"); /* System.out.print("B"); */ System.out.print("C");
items.a: Output: AC. Everything between /* and */ is a comment and is completely ignored by the compiler. System.out.print("B") is inside the block comment so it never executes. Only A and C are printed.

items.q: 5. What Javadoc tags would you write for a method: public double divide(double a, double b) that throws ArithmeticException when b is 0?
items.a: /** * Divides a by b. * @param a  the dividend * @param b  the divisor; must not be zero * @return   the result of {@code a / b} * @throws ArithmeticException if {@code b} is zero */. Key points: one @param per parameter, @return for the double result, @throws with the exact exception type and condition.

items.q: 6. Can you use // inside a /* */ block comment? Does it have any effect?
items.a: Yes, you can write // inside /* */, but it has absolutely no effect. Inside a /* */ block, everything is commented out until the */ delimiter — the // characters are just text and don't trigger anything. Example: /* this is all // comment until the star-slash */. The // only acts as a comment delimiter outside a block comment.

items.q: 7. You have a Java file with 500 lines and need to temporarily disable lines 200–250 for testing. What comment type would you use and why?
items.a: Multi-line comment (/* ... */). Wrap the block: add /* before line 200 and */ after line 250. This disables all 50 lines in one operation without touching each line individually. Exception: if lines 200–250 already contain /* */ comments inside, use // on each of those lines instead to avoid nested comment errors. Most IDEs let you select a block and press Ctrl+/ to auto-add // to each line.

items.q: 8. What command generates Javadoc HTML for Student.java with author and version info, outputting to a folder named 'apidocs'?
items.a: javadoc -d apidocs -author -version Student.java. Breakdown: javadoc = the tool, -d apidocs = destination directory for output HTML, -author = include @author tags in output, -version = include @version tags in output, Student.java = the source file to document. Open apidocs/index.html in a browser to view the generated documentation.

Wraps a block — starts /* ends */. Cannot be nested. Best for block explanations
Starts with ** — processed by javadoc tool to generate HTML docs. Supports @ tags

Comment WHY not WHAT. Keep comments short, accurate, and updated with code changes
Nesting /* */ comments — causes compile error. Use // to comment out code with /* */ inside
Do not leave commented-out code permanently — delete it and rely on Git history
